utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Judge Morrison is indisposed today, so we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I hope he can join us as soon as possible. Yes, Ms. West. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Katanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. West. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning Your Honours. I'm pleased to introduce Andjela Vuckovic, who is a native of Montenegro who has joined our team in the last few weeks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, when we broke off yesterday, you were talking about your long-standing relationship with Miroslav Deronjic. At this point, I want to turn your attention to the events in 1995 in Bratunac, and specifically in July of 1995. Now, during July and the months before, were you working for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I worked for the SDS as their technical secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was Miroslav Deronjic's position with the SDS at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic was the president of the party, and at the same time, he held other positions with the authorities. I think he was the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, on 11th July 1995, what appointment did Mr. Deronjic receive from President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic was appointed by President Karadzic to the position of civilian commissioner for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was placed in the 2nd Battalion as a private. When the Serb forces entered Srebrenica, Miroslav Deronjic summoned me and told me that he needed me in his office since he had been appointed civilian commissioner for Srebrenica. It was on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did he give you a specific task?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we saw each other, he told me to set up a meeting in the evening with the representatives of the Srebrenica municipality authorities as well as a certain number of people whom he wanted to appoint to positions of company managers, of both public institutions and companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And where was the meeting to be held?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was scheduled to take place in the large meeting hall of the SDS which could take in some 50 people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small intervention for the transcript. I understand the interpreters may have a peculiar economical system. They were not strictly private companies. They were public companies and socially or state-owned companies. They used to be called socially owned, whereas, as a matter of fact, it was -- they were owned by the state. It was line 2 -- line 25, page 2. Perhaps the witness could clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is an area you can clarify during your cross-examination. As translate -- not -- it says "... appoint to positions of company managers, some socially and some privately owned."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an error in the transcript, because that's not what the witness said. In my cross-examination, I will try to clarify with the witness the things he said, but I don't need to deal with transcript errors per se. In our system, there were public companies or public utility companies, and there -- then there were socially or state-owned companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I would like the CLSS to look into the -- that part and clarify, come up with clarification later on. Yes, Ms. West. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, about how many people attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't know exactly. More than 20, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And who chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by Mr. Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At some point in the meeting did Deronjic leave the room?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting, Miroslav Deronjic informed those present that he had been appointed civilian commissioner for the municipality of Srebrenica. During the meeting, the party secretary, Ms. Nikolic, arrived in the large meeting room and told Deronjic that President Karadzic was on the line. Miroslav Deronjic left to take the call, and after some time the secretary returned and invited us all to the room where the phone was. It was a small office, so we couldn't all fit in. We left the door open, and some people were out in the hallway. Then Miroslav Deronjic said that Mr. Karadzic wanted to say something that all of us should hear. Mr. Karadzic addressed all those present by saying that Miroslav Deronjic was responsible to him for all civilian affairs in the municipality of Srebrenica and that he is to guarantee for that with his life and that the other people were responsible to Miroslav Deronjic for their respective areas of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Had you ever heard President Karadzic's voice before?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a number of times. I heard President Karadzic's voice, although we never spoke on the phone directly. However, I could hear him speaking live. I heard him speak at some rallies through the loudspeakers or in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As a result of that phone call, what did you understand to be the professional relationship between Deronjic and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Karadzic addressed us on the phone, my conclusion was that the relationship was quite professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who did you understand Deronjic's superior to be? From whom would he at that point take orders?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leading question. It implies that he received orders. He was appointed rather than received orders. Where did the witness say that he received any orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who did you understand Deronjic's superior to be? From whom would he at that point take orders? No. We don't agree with it. Can you answer the question, Mr. Katanic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. The Chamber ruled it's not leading. Can you answer the question, Mr. Katanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miroslav Deronjic was appointed by President Karadzic. It was by wave of -- way of a written decision. By the fact of appointment, President Karadzic was his superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When we interviewed you, you drew a diagram of the SDS office, and we're going to talk about that in a moment, but I'd like you to draw another diagram on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I can have the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing that, Ms. West, could you ask the witness what an a technical secretary was and what he did in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, you heard the President's question which regarded your job. Can you tell us what you did in your role as a technical secretary?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Miroslav Deronjic was chosen to act as civilian commissioner for Srebrenica, I held the job of technical secretary. My job had to do with preparing meetings, setting them up, receiving people when President Deronjic was away from his office, and dealing with technical issues. It also included dealing with requests by people who came to the office, if they were founded.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say "technical issues," can you tell us a little bit more about that? What were technical issues?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it included the preparation of meetings which took place at party premises. Also, co-ordinating the work of the party itself with its local branches, as well as assisting them in their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when were you first -- when did you first start that job?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I no longer recall the date, but I think it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And was that a paid position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was placed in that position by a decision of the ministry as a work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When did you finish that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stopped working in that position when the war was over, but in 1993, shortly after being appointed to that position, I was sent by the military command of the municipality of Bratunac to another front line where I spent some two months as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in July of 1995, when you were working as a technical secretary at the SDS office, can you tell us how often you were present in the SDS office itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, before Mladic's arrival in Bratunac, I spent the regular working hours in the office, that is to say from 7.00 to 3.00 p.m. When Miroslav Deronjic was appointed civilian commissioner for Srebrenica, there were no longer any working hours. I was in the office all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's talk about the office itself. When we spoke to you, you made a diagram in the office, but at this point on the screen in front of you I'd like you to draw a diagram of the office, but I want you to include the conference room where you said you had the meeting on July 11th. If you can include that as well, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you indicate the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The 65 ter number of the previous office diagram you did was 23555. It now has a Prosecution exhibit number. This diagram, Mr. Katanic, I hope will be a little bit different. It will be a bit broader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking because we don't have a diagram before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I'm asking the witness if he will draw us one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On a blank page.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: On a blank page or on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That should be possible. Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Katanic, on the screen in front of you, you can take the pen and you can actually draw a diagram of the SDS, but in this diagram I'd like you to include the conference room.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this enough?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We'll go through it together. Now, on the top right-hand side of the drawing you have some words, and they are pointed to the room in the top-hand side of the drawing. What are -- what does at that say?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Secretary's office."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And the office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can you change the colour of the pen into blue. Could you put the number 1 on that so we don't need the translation right now. In the meantime I noted that 65 ter 23555, the diagram which witness drew earlier on, we need translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Could you put number 1 on secretary room above the B/C/S writing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the office below the secretary's office that we see on the screen, whose office was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was President Deronjic's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you put a number 2 above the writing that is indicating Deronjic's office.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out what you wrote there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Deronjic's office."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, if we go outside number 1, the secretary's office, is that a hallway?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you've put some writing in that area as well. Can you tell us what that -- what the writing says.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote "Hallway."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. If you can put a 3 above that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, there's another room on the left hand of the screen, to the extreme left. Can you tell us what room that is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the large meeting or conference room of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you have some writing in that room as well, and can you tell us exactly what the writing says.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also wrote "The large meeting room of the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Put a -- please put a 4 on top of that writing.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we change the colour of the pen one more time, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, we talked about this meeting on July 11th that Mr. Deronjic asked you to organise, and you said that it was in the SDS office. The meeting that took place with the 20-plus people, which room was that in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in room number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you testified that at some point you left that room to listen to a telephone call. Where did you go to listen to that telephone call?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't leave the room. Mr. Deronjic did, because he was called by the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. At any point -- well, you testified that you heard Mr. Karadzic on the telephone. In which room was that telephone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The telephone was in office number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So at some point did all the people in office number 4 go to office number 1?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you describe for us - you mentioned it was a number - where all these people were located in and around office number 1. You can do it with your pen.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Some people entered office number 1 and others remained in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Could you write the date of today, which is 10th of February, 2012, and your initial on the right bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's save this first. We'll admit it as the next P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4380, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And after saving it, we upload it and zoom it on room number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's zoom it in further on room number 1. That's a bit too much. Is it okay? Ms. West, I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We are now looking at room number 1 where you indicated - right there's perfect. Thank you - was located the phone where you heard Karadzic's voice, and I asked you about the people who came into that room. Can you indicate on this -- you can still write on this. Can you indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you wait until assisted by the usher. The usher needs to sets up the pen. Probably in black.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now I'd like you to tell us, show us, where in and about this office all the participants of the conference you had called were located during the telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This area marked green would roughly be the area where the attendees of the meeting were, those who listened to Mr. Karadzic's conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you put an X where the telephone was located.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may this be the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you initial and date this drawing, Mr. Katanic. This will be Exhibit P4381.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I mark that little cross -- actually, should I write down that that denotes the telephone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Could you put your initial and date somewhere between the two numbers 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be saved. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, you had testified that you and Mr. Deronjic spoke to each other frequently in the evenings. Can you tell us again in the month of July -- or in that period of time, in the month of June and July, where these conversations would take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the situation that prevailed in Bratunac at the time, I saw Miroslav Deronjic quite seldom during our free time, because I didn't have much free time and he had even less. All of our conversations took place in passing at SDS offices. However, before these events, during our free time, often, almost every day, I would see Miroslav Deronjic at the Caesar cafe that I owned, and in the evening, we would tell each other about what happened during that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 72 of your statement, you noted that you became aware of the July 13th killings at Kravica warehouse on that same night, July 13th. How did you become aware of them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I heard about that from Miroslav Deronjic at the SDS office. He told me about that, although he was not aware of any details either. He had just heard that that happened. Judging by the way he said this to me, my conclusion was that this was something that had worried him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd now like to go to 65 ter 40246A. This is a video. We will play it, but there's also an accompanying transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, this is a video you've seen before. It's dated July 14th, 1995. It's a newscast. We're just going to walk -- we're going to go through it, and then I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go through this. I just want you to ID some people, and if you'll bear with me, we'll play it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I just stopped at -- I've just stopped at 1 minute and 1 second.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is on July 14th, and the announcer has just noted that Serbian refugees who had left the area more than two years ago are coming back too. Were you aware that Serbians refugees were returning to Srebrenica after its take-over?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, there was no organised return to Srebrenica. However, there were inhabitants of Srebrenica who lived in Bratunac, and they, that is correct, went to their houses to see what they were like, and on the following days, they went to Srebrenica again and they cleaned their own houses, because it was impossible to enter Srebrenica and go on living in Srebrenica. Srebrenica had to be brought into order, if you will, because it was in very bad shape. The living conditions there were basically non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, do you know SRT television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Serb Radio Television that was broadcast from Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the title on the right side, how does it read? Could you read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "News, Serb Television."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this particular Serb Radio Television that was broadcasted, this programme, had you ever seen this programme before?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And let me clarify my question. I don't specifically mean this programme but this newscast. Were you familiar with this newscast or this station?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of that TV station. That is Serb Radio Television, and it was very popular among the Serb people. People watched this programme, the news, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We will continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, we've stopped at 1 minute and 27 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you identify the people in this frame?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person on the left is Mr. Miroslav Deronjic. Next to him, in the middle, is Dane Katanic. He was a member of the Municipal Board of the Serb Democratic Party, and I think that he was the president Executive Board for the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is he related to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's a relative of mine. The third person, with a beard, I think his name is Milenko, and his last name is Canic, and I think that he was president of the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 1 minute and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you recognise this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is Momcilo Krajisnik. He was president of the Assembly, the people's Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And earlier in this video, and I'm going to try to avoid going back, there was a person who was sitting to the left of Mr. Karadzic. Do you recognise that person? He was at the same table as Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now. Was it also Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik? I'm not sure. If it could be shown again, I could identify that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'll do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We started at 1:20 and we've stopped at 1:21.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The person on the right, do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person on right is Momcilo Cvjetinovic. He was president of the party in Srebrenica, the president of the Serb Democratic Party in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 2 minutes and 25 seconds, and this is an interview with Deronjic, and he's talking about the state of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, right after the attack on Srebrenica, or at least in the month of July, did you have an opportunity to go to Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Srebrenica only seven days after it had been liberated. At the time, Srebrenica was in very poor shape. It was in such a bad condition that, believe me, I didn't even leave the car. People who had already been to Srebrenica were warning us not to get out in order to avoid getting some kind of a disease. It was extremely dirty and there were lice in town, so I just drove around in my car and went back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we're -- here Mr. Deronjic says the town was quite ruined, destroyed, and plundered. Is that consistent with your memory as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town was quite destroyed, that is correct. Also, there had been cases of looting, and the task of the civilian commissioner was - and I helped him in carrying out this task - to prevent this looting in the following way: Directors of public institutions and public utilities were appointed, and they made inventories of the property there. They also introduced guard duty in various companies, and they started cleaning the buildings that these companies were in, and the public utilities started cleaning the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll play till the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just for record, we did have subtitles, but also we have transcript which is attached to the e-court; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted as the next P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4382, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just becoming a little bit concerned about the time. I know you've allocated three and a half hours to Dr. Karadzic for his cross-examination, and if it were to begin immediately we would end at 3.00 with that three and a half hours, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, do we have to finish this witness's evidence by today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know what his situation is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd have to inquire. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just asking what prompted your concerns, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, normally we try to complete the testimony of a witness before the weekend, so I was just concerned that if he wasn't able to stay over the weekend Dr. Karadzic doesn't lose his allotted time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll ask the witness. Mr. Katanic, is it your case that you need to return before the weekend, or more directly, whether you can stay over the weekend till Monday next week.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the court is my first priority, but I would appreciate it very much if I could go back on Sunday, because it's my daughter's birthday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My daughter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My daughter is young. She's only 12 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No doubt she will miss you. We'll see how it evolves, but let's carry on. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have 65 ter 23556, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, you've seen these before. It's a few pages long. It's five or six pages long, and these are bills from the Hotel Fontana. And looking at the first page with the stamp on it, what -- what can you tell us about this piece of paper? Is this familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an invoice issued by the state-owned hotel company Podrinje in Bratunac. It was issued to the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac for the services rendered. I saw this invoice for the first time when the Prosecution showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know anything about how these -- how invoices to the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac were paid? Do you know anything about that process?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object. Let Madam Prosecutor establish with this witness whether the invoice was paid. It was issued, but we don't know if it was paid and how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I read the question again: "Do you know anything about how these -- how invoices to the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac were paid? Do you know anything about that process?" I don't see anything that you should be concerned about. If witness knows, he can answer the question. But before that, was the name of that state-owned hotel company Podrinje in Bratunac Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Fontana Hotel was part of this company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, Mr. Katanic, can you answer the question from Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the question was: Do you know anything about invoices to the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac were paid? Do you know anything about that process?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Bratunac had its functioning account. It was customary that the president of the Executive Council paid such invoices. At the time, I did not work at the municipality. As I said, I saw this invoice for the first time when shown it by the Prosecution. Therefore, there's nothing else I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies, good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Katanic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to help me shed some light on some parts which drew my attention in the transcript. First of all, you mentioned work obligation. That is when someone is ordered to do something irrespective of whether they're employed somewhere or not. And was this service to be performed instead of a compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It was a military assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It applies to everyone, including yourself and SDS officials?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We need to wait for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would propose that it be translated as it was in the past, "compulsory work" rather than "work obligation." It occurred in the testimony of some Muslim witnesses, and the impression was that it only applied to them. In such cases, it was translated as "compulsory work," whereas today we have "work obligation." It was on page 6, lines 23 and 24. I suggest that the other option be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's for the CLSS, but I will ask them to take a look into that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us begin with the footage as one of the last things we dealt with. Do you agree that at 02, Mr. Deronjic said that he also came to ask for help? Do you agree that material assistance could only be provided by the Assembly and that the president of the government -- of the republic had no such powers? Did they not come asking for help from the government?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at 02 -- sorry, 2:25 onwards, Mr. Deronjic invited all former residents to return? He didn't only invite the Serbs to return. If you wish, we can go back to the footage.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need. I observed his statement, and it is true that he invited all former residents of Srebrenica to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the war was over, did some Muslims and Serbs return, and is it true that not all Muslims or Serbs returned?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the fighting stopped, no one returned to stay in Srebrenica. They returned for a while to clean their homes, because in the town itself, there was no water or electricity. They simply came to prepare their homes to be able to live there. Only when all the conditions were finally met, that is when organised return started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who returned?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs returned to their homes. There were also some refugees from Central Bosnia, mostly from Ilijas and other places. They were placed in the empty apartments and houses. During that period of time, I know of no Muslim returns. They began returning only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Muslims began returning when the peace agreement was signed and that before there were no conditions in place for them to return?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that they only started returning after the peace agreement was signed, but not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it depend on the Serb authorities or their own feeling of safety?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended exclusively on their own feeling of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the moment when the peace agreement was signed until today, is it not the case that some of the most prominent position -- positions in the Srebrenica authorities are held by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The president -- or, rather, head of municipality of Srebrenica is a Muslim. In terms of political structure, the head of municipality, one may say, holds the greatest executive powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it differ from the previous system where the President of the Municipal Assembly held the highest authority and the head of municipality, as is nowadays called mayor, was the person number two?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We heard Mr. Deronjic mention, informing the President about the military situation. Do you recall that after their visit, I declared a state of war on the 14th of July in Birac and some other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were Mr. Deronjic and his delegation right in saying to me that things were not over and that in the forests there were enormous numbers of Muslim soldiers and that they would be able to capture any settlement they could and that a state of war needs to be proclaimed so as to safeguard the population and institutions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of territory, Srebrenica is one of the largest municipalities of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. It covers an enormous area. As for any groups of Muslims who did not want to surrender or go to Tuzla together with the group which did remained hidden for quite some time in the area of the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that I was told that there was still no victory there, although they entered Srebrenica on the 11th? I was also told that a state of war should be proclaimed. Is it correct that in Bratunac itself people were afraid because there were no Serb soldiers in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are three questions in there. If I could just ask that this be more simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you break down your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted for Mr. Katanic to be on time for his daughter's birthday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, I will try to put questions which will largely -- which could largely be answered with a yes or no, and of course you're free to expand if you want to. Is it correct that Muslims could enter any Serb town in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I understand your question. What time do you have in mind when you say that they could walk into any town? Do you mean the period before the 12th of July or after the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the Muslim forces that were scattered throughout the woods. Is it correct that in Bratunac, and you talked about this in paragraph 79, you say that they were scattered all around, while in town there were only teenagers and people over 70 years old, whereas the Bratunac Brigade moved on towards Zepa. So is it correct that Bratunac was defenseless at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that Bratunac had very few able-bodied persons at the time, and it is true that I expressed my fear, but that related to something quite different. That was a reference to the time when the prisoners were in the town, when they were in different streets. They were all over town on streets, and they presented a threat to the town. As for your question, the groups that remained scattered throughout the territory of Srebrenica municipality that did not want to surrender or join the convoys on route to Tuzla, they could pose a threat in that they could commit an atrocity or a crime somewhere. They could loot a house or two, but these were not homogeneous large groups that could pose a threat to the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now take a look at a document showing what the DB stated about that. Could we see 65 ter 1959.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we've disclosed this to the Prosecution or notified the Prosecution that we'd be using this document. If not, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this portion which says that Pobudje and Bratunac municipalities, there's still present, a large group around 500 armed men, and allegedly in the course of the next evening they were planning a breakthrough of the Milici-Konjevic Polje-Drinjaca road, and so on. So do you agree that this is a report sent to the Ministry of the Interior of Sarajevo by the state security department? We see that it's a document signed by the head of the state security. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that. This report referred to the group that was moving towards Tuzla. That was a group that was being observed, but what I referred to a moment ago were smaller groups that were not organised and that remained even after the signing of the agreement remained in the territory of Srebrenica scattered. Now, this is a reference to a group that was moving from Srebrenica towards Tuzla. These were able-bodied men, armed men, and a group of civilians also joined them, civilians who refused to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2058, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were asked about the television is it correct that this was about the state television and that there was a window from the Sarajevo studio, whereas the other window or frame was from the Banja Luka studio? We saw at the very beginning that there were two windows.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I -- this is probably correct. I did watch the Serbian TV occasionally, because we had -- we could not receive other TVs at Bratunac, and I knew that it was broadcast from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this was the latest thing that you saw. So probably on the 11th you could have heard my voice? Now, do you know that there was a conversation between me and Mr. Deronjic on this day, but because the lines were down the conversation was actually conducted via a mediator, a third party? Did you -- were you present during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I did know that there was such a possibility, that Deronjic and you would communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during this conversation that you listened in on or listened to, did Deronjic receive any instructions or was he encouraged in any way to do anything that would be against the law in his function as the civilian commissioner?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deronjic, as the civilian commissioner, had a strict obligation to take care of civilians, of their property, and also to handle civilian affairs in Srebrenica. Other than that, he had no powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that an alternative to the civilian commissioner in a town that is without an organised government, the only alternative would have been military control and that this would be a normal way of establishing authority in a newly captured territory, and that by appointing Deronjic, I, in fact, sidestepped or tried to avoid the military role?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam West implied today that in one of her questions she asked you about who was Deronjic's superior and whom he received orders from. Did you ever learn who Deronjic received orders from, and did he receive records from anyone or did he just act as the situation demanded?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By -- when he was appointed civilian commissioner, Deronjic had the powers and the authority to take action within that ambit. Other than that, I am not aware that there was any pressure put on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether he received any orders on a daily or a weekly basis which would be outside of the legal framework within which he could work together with the authorities of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I see what time it is. Do we need to go on break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I'm just asking for a clarification of the record. Shortly before we broke, there -- in the record Mr. Karadzic was asking the witness about a conversation, and I think we can see that on the screen now. Yeah. Exactly. This would be page 26, and this starts -- will begin on 18. The witness was talking about the video, the television video, and then at 21 Mr. Karadzic said: "Now, this was the latest thing that you saw," and that would be the 14th, "so probably on the 11th you could have heard my voice." And then he says: Now do you know that there was a conversation between me and Mr. Deronjic on this day, but because the lines were down, it was via a mediator. So the clarification I'm looking for is what Mr. Karadzic meant "on this day," and the reason this is an issue is because he's talking about a conversation between a mediator and I assume he must mean a conversation on the 13th, because there is evidence that Mr. Karadzic had a conversation with Mr. Deronjic through a mediator on the 13th. And just two days ago Mr. Karadzic asked (redacted) some questions about this as well, and this is two days ago transcript 24257, talking about the conversation on the 11th. (redacted) gives an answer. But then at line 14 Mr. Karadzic says: "We do have evidence that it was through an intermediary." So the result of all of this is today when Mr. Karadzic said "this day." I just need a clarification, and I assume it must be the 13th if he means the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was it? What's the date of all the people hearing Mr. Karadzic's voice as to the appointment of Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That is on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before speaking about my understanding, can I hear from you, Mr. Karadzic on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. I believe that what I said was not recorded in the transcript. Did you also hear the conversation that I had on the 13th via a mediator? And I said, You probably heard my voice on the 11th, but were you present during the conversation that I had through an intermediary on the 13th? So it is indubitable that the conversation was on the 13th. I believe that on the 14th Deronjic was -- came to see me, and there was no occasion to talk to him because he left Bratunac early to -- to come and see me in my office. Now -- so there is a portion missing here where it says, You probably heard my voice on the 11th, but do you remember that there was also a conversation through an intermediary because the lines were down on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you satisfied, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katanic. Please make yourself comfortable. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we talked about the conversation that you heard and listened to. Did you understand that Deronjic wanted you to hear that he was appointed to this post which would then vest him the -- in the authority that he needed in order to carry out that function?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could interpret it that way. Could you say it's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you prepared that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you invited all former members, Serb officials, and in this joint Assembly as well as Serb officials in the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica that existed for a while; correct? In other words, people who were in the local government in the past and then fled.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. So people -- also people who were managers of companies and officials and state institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So Deronjic's task was to ensure continuity of the government. In other words, to ensure that there was a local government in the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that point in time on the 11th in the evening we did not know that all Muslims would leave? But before that, my question: Do you agree that it could be expected that those people who were not from Srebrenica, who were not locals, would -- it would be normal to expect them to leave Srebrenica, people from Cerska and other places?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time in Srebrenica, the population had swelled because people came from other municipalities to Srebrenica. We could not assume with any certainty that the entire population of Srebrenica would leave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that became evident only on the 12th of July after a series of meetings with UNPROFOR, with Mladic, and with Muslims' representatives?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a decision that the Muslim people took, and they expressed this decision through their representatives who attended the meeting at the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get back to this later. Now, let me ask you this: Was there any dilemma that Deronjic was in charge and trusted with establishing civilian authorities in Srebrenica and that none of those applied to Srebrenica? In other words, that he did not have any authority in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deronjic was appointed civilian commissioner of the municipality of Srebrenica and that applied to Srebrenica alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in Bratunac, the legal authorities continued in their work, and Deronjic did not have any authority over them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by being appointed civilian commissioner in Srebrenica municipality, he did not get any special powers for the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked, but you also said in paragraph 71 of your amalgamated statement, and I don't know if you have that translated into Serbian, you were asked about various options, whether Deronjic could have talked to me from some other place, and you said that such a possibility did exist, but then there was something else. You were asked whether you knew whether Deronjic had informed me of the Kravica incident on the 13th of July when he came to see me on the 14th of July. You said that you didn't know anything about that, but that as far as you knew him, that would be possible because some of those people were civilians and others were combatants. So now let me ask you this: Before he left for Pale early in the morning on the 14th, was there any other matter that Deronjic could need to inform me about? Were there any other dramatic incidents, murders, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You learned on the 14th, after you arrived at work or in the course of that day, of the bodies found in the school building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that from my family and that because my school was in the vicinity of -- my house was in the vicinity of the school building, and that's how we learned that some people had been killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 72 and onwards, you talk about -- for instance, in 82, and I will read the entire paragraph in English: [In English] "The next day, the Muslim prisoners were taken away from Bratunac. I did not see them leave. I heard from the public media that most of the prisoners were taken to Zvornik municipality. Probably some were taken to other places. I don't think there is anyone from Bratunac who could help them. Miroslav Deronjic tried to keep the honour of Bratunac to avoid them being imprisoned here."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For the record, that's paragraph 83.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you saw for yourself that Deronjic did not want them to be kept there, and at that point in time no one had any idea about the killings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to refer to the summary of my statement that was read out by the Prosecutor where she said something to the effect that those people were murdered. However, in all my statements so far, I have said that in this particular case the issue was the imprisonment of these prisoners of war in Bratunac, because all these prisoners were arrested in different municipalities and then were brought to Bratunac and only to Bratunac. I said that I thought that Mr. Karadzic helped Deronjic because these prisoners were not detained in Bratunac, or they shouldn't be detained in Bratunac, but, rather, be distributed throughout various municipalities and that -- because this would be a great burden for the Bratunac municipality, which was already encumbered with a lot of financial difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph that's what you mention. Now, do you remember that Mr. Deronjic was angry with Mr. Dukic because the prisoners who were arrested in his municipality were being sent to Bratunac? In paragraph 94, you say talk about that, but you don't mention Dukic, but rather Milici. Do you remember that that was the reason why he was angry, why they weren't kept in his own municipality but rather sent to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I was trying to describe a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know by any chance that an order had been sent -- or, rather, a message that a thousand people should be received at Batkovic and that in Rogatica also there should be facilities prepared for the reception of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. However, Miroslav Deronjic told me that he had major problems with Lieutenant-Colonel Beara. He didn't want them detained on the territory of Bratunac municipality, and when they were bused out of Bratunac, I said that I thought that Mr. Karadzic had helped him in persuading Beara to send them to a different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Deronjic tell you that as part of that argument he told him he would go to Pale the next day and speak to the president about it all and that that is what finally persuaded Beara to give up on accommodating the prisoners in the brickworks factory or at another location?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Batkovic was the only well-known POW camp after Manjaca and that people were exchanged from there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We touched upon this topic during the previous session. You said that the people in Bratunac were upset because of the presence of so many prisoners. They were restless. Is it correct that only those who were not fit for military service guarded those prisoners so as to protect them from anyone who would want to take revenge on them, and by the same token, they were there to safeguard the town from the prisoners themselves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was in the office when concerned citizens came in. They were concerned for their safety, because there were a great many prisoners in the town, on the buses and trucks, which were not guarded appropriately. I informed the police station about that, and then they took upon themselves to provide additional security, because the army had gone on to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there was a small number of people who guarded the prisoners? And I'm looking for a specific paragraph. Somewhere you said that if they had known how poorly Bratunac was secured, they could have rioted.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Some additional guards were provided by the so-called third wave of draftees who were otherwise people who were not -- deemed not fit for military service and were usually not called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you notice that the civilian protection of Bratunac undertook some measures to take care of those people, civilians, in Potocari as well as providing water to the prisoners who were on the buses? Do you have anything to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal authorities took measures through their services so that the prisoners were provided with the basic necessities, including those who were on the buses as well as in Potocari. In other words, they brought food and water for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: When did you realise that something would be going on around Srebrenica? Is it correct that you only realised that once you saw the army coming in great numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not realise that there would be anything done around Srebrenica for quite some time. I believe the operation was well underway by the time one could conclude that it was aimed at Srebrenica. A few days before the entry into Srebrenica, Miroslav Deronjic left without notifying anyone in the party. He went to the forward command post called Pribicevac. He spent three days there without returning to Bratunac. Only once he returned did he tell me that there was an operation around Srebrenica underway. At around that time, General Mladic arrived in Bratunac as well. All able-bodied men who were included in work obligations reported to their war assignment locations. I, too, went to the 2nd Battalion, because General Mladic was well known for his dislike of men fit for military service walking around town. When General Mladic arrived in Bratunac, it dawned on me only then that Srebrenica will be tackled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting. But page 29 today, lines 5 and 7, my earlier comments. Can we have a redaction for lines 5 and 7 before it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. It's your submission. Yes. Thank you. Shall we continue from there? You can take up, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wasn't able to identify what this is about, but I do not object to a redaction if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to draw your attention to paragraph 93. I'll read it out in English: [In English] "Deronjic stated that at that moment Beara was searching for a location, probably to kill the prisoners, right in Bratunac. And I think Deronjic was assisted by Karadzic so that these prisoners were relocated from Bratunac and were not killed in Bratunac. I think that because on one side there was a military leadership in Bratunac represented by Mladic and his high-level officer Beara, and on the other side there were civilian representative Deronjic, and I think he, by himself, could not defend himself and impose his will on a Main Staff colonel of VRS." [Interpretation] I would like to clarify something. Is this the way you formulated this sentence because you subsequently learned of the killings, or did you at that moment know that it was Beara's request that they be either killed or imprisoned there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to the summary of my statement presented by Madam Prosecutor. What I said is that I had not stated it previously. It only appeared in the abbreviated version. I always state -- I have always stated that the issue at hand was imprisonment. At the time, it was not known that they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload his amalgamated statement. Page 18 in hard copy, para 93.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ninety-one, 92, 93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me -- just a second. In para 92, the first sentence reads like this, Mr. Katanic: "Deronjic said that Beara sent people to search for places where they could imprison Muslim prisoners in the brick factory and Sase mines." But 93 reads -- para 93 reads like this, I'll read it for you: "Deronjic stated that at that moment, Beara was searching for a location, probably to kill the prisoners, right in Bratunac. And I think that Deronjic was assisted by Karadzic so that these prisoners were relocated from Bratunac and were not killed in Bratunac." Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic asked question about this para 93. Mr. Karadzic, could you ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 93 and 92, you say that at that point in time the civilian authorities were asked to provide a place where the people would be imprisoned, and all of a sudden in paragraph 93 we have this reference to a place that would be used to probably kill the prisoners. Was it clear at that time that they would be killed, or did this find its way in the -- into the paragraph because of something you learned subsequently, that there were killings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having stated this in paragraph 93. I did sign the document, the statement, but I need to say that I signed the document without having a Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- which refers to killing, probably killing, has a citation which refers to your interview. Would you like to see them, or do we have an audiotape?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is directly from an interview. I believe we have it in B/C/S, but these -- these footnotes are direct quotes from the interview itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So I'm asking Mr. Katanic whether he's interested in seeing the interview you had -- you had with the Prosecutor. Is it correct, interview with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think there is any need. I trust this. But perhaps the question was put in such a leading way that my answer came out as it did without thinking about the weight of what I said, and now I realise its full weight. It is a fact that it happened. The killings ensued. But at that time, as we can see from the previous paragraph, I was not discussing any killings, because I did not have this idea or expectation that the prisoners would be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to reserve my question at the end, but I have to intervene now. Could you -- could we take a look at para 43 -- I'm sorry, 83 again, the previous page. At the end of this paragraph you said,

utterances.speaker: MR. KATANIC
utterances.text: "Miroslav Deronjic tried to keep the honour of Bratunac to avoid them being imprisoned here." My question for you, Mr. Katanic, is this: Why would Bratunac be dishonoured if it was to keep -- if it was to imprison the prisoners? I would understand if the prisoners were to be killed in Bratunac it may dishonour Bratunac, or I can understand it would be a burden for Bratunac to imprison them, but it's a bit difficult to understand why Bratunac would be dishonoured by imprisoning those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Your Honour, the prisoners were those who had surrendered voluntarily because the police went around with loudspeakers calling out to the masses that were moving from Srebrenica to Tuzla, asking them to surrender, saying that their safety and security would be guaranteed and that the Serb army guaranteed that they would be safe, that nothing would happen to them. In these columns of people who were surrendering, there were quite a few civilians, probably people who did not -- who do not deserve this treatment of being prisoners of war. Probably that had to do with that. That was the honour involved. It is possible that when this interview was conducted, it was well known what had happened, all of it, and it's been almost 20 years -- or, rather, this happened almost 20 years after these events. When it was known that these prisoners were being killed, perhaps the statement was made in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katanic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're on the subject, let me ask you this as well: Did Bratunac have an appropriate infrastructure for properly, in accordance with the law, put up such large number of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bratunac did have an infrastructure, but not for putting them up properly. This would not have satisfied even the most minimal criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that perhaps the question was a leading one. I want to ask you the following: How were your answers formulated? Were they transcripted from the -- transcribed from the tape directly, or did someone help you in the formulation of the answers you gave during this interview?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interview was audio recorded, and it was typed up on a typewriter. One of the investigators typed it up in English. After the interview, I was given that to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you speak the English language?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say no, because I know a few words only. It's not even sufficient for getting by in a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph -- actually, on page -- actually, paragraphs 83 and 4 and onwards. And you assume that my authority helped, because you believe that Deronjic could not oppose a member of the Main Staff on his own. You also confirm that Deronjic had not informed you about this but that he managed to prevent this from happening in Bratunac, the detention, I mean, and you assumed that that happened because he invoked my name; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that he had your assistance in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. So that is paragraph 93 that refers to that; right? [In English] "Deronjic did not tell me that he received support from Karadzic in having prisoners moved out of Bratunac. Deronjic never told me about any conversation he may have had with Karadzic about the fate of the Muslim prisoners in Bratunac or about Deronjic speaking with Beara. I do not know if Deronjic did or did not discuss these topics with Karadzic. If Karadzic told Deronjic that all the Muslims should be killed, as I read in the newspaper, I find it strange that he would not have told me about it. [Interpretation] Are you convinced of this, that you had said that if I had told Deronjic that they should be killed, Deronjic would have certainly told you about it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit strange considering the kind of person Deronjic was who liked to say, I was with Karadzic today, or, Today I talked to Mr. Karadzic, because this gave him importance too. After all, not everybody could talk to Mr. Karadzic. And when he says, I talked to Mr. Karadzic, then that gives him a certain wait. That is why I stated that he, as a person who liked to say something that he talked about with Karadzic, he never said that to me, and he never said that to anyone in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, had I known that we would have been discussing this subject, I would have brought something. Did you know that the late Professor Koljevic, actually, that his diary was published after his death, "The Creation of Republika Srpska," two volumes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you that Koljevic also wrote that he met up with our civilian commissioner a month or a month and a half later and asked him what it was that really happened in Srebrenica, he says that Deronjic said to him, Professor, nothing. Do you find that understandable? Is this in accordance with what you said in terms of what he would say and what he would not say?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this conversation with Mr. Koljevic, I hadn't heard about that, and it doesn't really mean much to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you expect Deronjic to say that? Is that in accordance with what you know in terms of what Deronjic was saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection. He's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I'm going to tender that diary at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In one of these paragraphs you say that these buses with the prisoners were leaving, and no one knew what their fate would be; right? That's paragraph 91. You say that even Miroslav did not know what would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the citizens of Bratunac and those who took part in escorting the buses to their destination did not know what the fate of the prisoners would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it was natural for them to head towards Zvornik and Bijeljina because Batkovic is near Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I didn't know what their destination was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know whether you've dealt with this. How did you find out -- or, rather, did you find out what caused that killing at the co-operative in Kravica on the 13th of July, 1995? Did you hear how that happened? Had that been prepared and planned or did something happen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for what happened in Kravica, I heard about that from Deronjic the same evening, but only by way of conveying information, because he was not aware of any details either. Later on, I found out that the cause of this was an incident that occurred roughly as follows: One of the prisoners seized an automatic rifle from a guard and killed another guard. That is why things happened the way they did. Now, whether that could have been prevented or kept under control, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any knowledge as to how many guards were guarding these people in Kravica at the co-operative there when this man dared seize a rifle and shoot?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge before or after; as to the number of guards, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of this being people who had been taken prisoner in the area of Sandici during the course of the day, or did anyone give you a reliable number as to how many persons were there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out -- actually, was it the duty of the civilian protection to bury the bodies, and did you hear of these killed persons being buried as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian protection was duty-bound to carry out the sanitisation of the terrain. I don't know if they were buried and, if so, at which location.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4098. Can we have a look at that, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in 1992, the president of the municipal government -- or, rather, the Executive Committee of the municipality was Mr. Rodoljub Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document. Would you agree that this was an order issued on the 25th of June, 1992, and it talks about the description of the locations where people who were killed in Bratunac and its surroundings, in other words, on the territory of the municipality, should be buried?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that it says here that after the bodies are identified, they should be buried either in accordance with the will of the families or -- would you like to read it? Should I give you some time to read through this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
