utterances.text: Well, I've read it. This order is an order saying that the bodies of people of Muslim ethnicities should be buried in the cemetery -- Muslim cemeteries; whereas people of the Orthodox faith, the Serb people, should be buried in Orthodox cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. However, there were so many casualties that it was impossible to comply with this order; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we see the next page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] English, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a standard document of a municipal government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the relevance, Mr. Karadzic? How is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is obvious that the municipal authorities in Bratunac took care, when they realised that there would be a war, took care of the matter of dealing with the burial of people who get killed. So this shows what the authorities did and what their responsibilities were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2059, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get back to the events of 1995 after the break. For now, I would just like to go back to the beginning of the crisis and the events between 1990 and 1992, and I'd like to ask you this: Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, for planning purpose, today we'll have a second break only for 50 minutes. I appreciate the understanding and indulgence of the staff. So we'll go till 12.40 to have a break, just to let you know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do we then go on to 3.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After the break. But I would like you to come back to 1995 as soon as possible. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was actually commending Dr. Karadzic for taking my advice this time. I told him to go to the most important things first, so I think we've used -- most of 1995 is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If there's anything else left over from 1995, I'll get back to that after the break, but now I'd like to touch upon these other subjects, and the witness is kind enough to answer concisely and briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree, Mr. Katanic, that in the previous system there was a one-party system in which Serbs and Muslims in Bratunac shared in the local government?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they shared in the local government under the auspices of the League of Communists, which was the only party in existence at the time, and the witness said yes, that that was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Party of Democratic Action was established first at the republic level and then in the Bratunac municipality followed by the establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, and you mentioned this in one of the paragraphs, that the people who had been for many years dissidents or in the opposition, or in any case, anti-Communists, were the ones who actually signed up to become members of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that Miroslav Deronjic and I were people who had not been politically active before the establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party. I can also state that in the beginning, many people joined the Serbian Democratic Party from among the ranks of politically disengaged people, not active, up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that Mr. Deronjic had a reputation even before the establishment of these new parties, that he had a certain reputation in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic was a teacher. He was a teacher of literature in Srebrenica municipality, and he worked in the school library. He was a very respectable citizen and had a very good reputation in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that before the establishment of these parties, he had a public appearance - this was while the League of Communists was still there - which actually created or established his reputation, because he opposed and he pointed out all the different machinations and the things that Communists were trying to do in order to maintain power?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it exactly that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, would you please say it in your own words?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The League of Communists, before the first multi-party parliamentary elections, organised a public debate, the topic of which I cannot recall, I'm not aware of it any more, but I know that Miroslav Deronjic and I were both present. This public debate had as its speakers some people from Sarajevo who toed the party line and who spoke for about two hours, which irritated Miroslav Deronjic, who then took the floor, and in three sentences he said far more than all the other speakers combined for the previous two hours. That left a deep impression on me, because I didn't know that face of Miroslav Deronjic. He probably left the same impression on all the other people who attended this public debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that decisive in Deronjic's profiling as the future leader, local leader, and is it correct, as you state in paragraph 11, that Karadzic even knew about -- or of Deronjic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. -- that Mr. Karadzic knew of Mr. Deronjic at the time, but at that time, the SDA and HDZ parties had already been established at the republic level. It was rumoured in the town that the Serb people, too, should organise themselves politically. So there were various gatherings organised where people talked about establishing an initiating board which would then organise the Serbian Democratic Party in Bratunac. One day when we were playing cards on the Drina, on the banks of the Drina, at a motel, after I heard about one such gathering I told Miroslav that perhaps we, too, should go and see what it was all about. He agreed, and from that point onward his fate was closely tied to that of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to put my questions in such a way that would allow you to answer with a yes or no. Is it correct that the initiative to establish the Serbian Democratic Party arose because there was a -- because there was a sense that the Serbs, too, needed to do something that the Croats and Muslim had already done and that it was not imposed from above but, rather, from grassroots?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bratunac that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that they did not manage to ensure my presence for the Assembly that actually put -- established the party and that I did not attend?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I was very sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that no one from the republic level interfered in the election of members of the Municipal Board and the municipal officials or the president of the party at the -- at the municipal level? Is it correct that no one interfered in that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We self-organised without any assistance from the republic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 12, you talk about how there was insufficient understanding for you at the republic level. Would it be more precise to say that there -- the presence and assistance from the federal and republic level was not sufficient and was not sufficiently present in -- in your local circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than the assistance that we got from Mr. Micevic - I believe that was his name - which consisted of some propaganda, flags, buttons and similar, there was no other assistance or support from the republic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you could say you established the party single-handedly, and that you won in the election single-handedly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at first, as you put it yourself, the powers were also shared between Serbs and Muslims but without the patronage of -- without the patronage of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the elections, the Serbian Democratic Party and the SDA, as the parties who one in the elections, shared in the local government. You could say that we were coalition partners and everything was normal. We both had, as our ideological opponent, the League of Communists, or as it was later known, the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that power was shared in accordance with good customs? If the president of the municipality was a Muslim, then the president of the Executive Board would be a Serb. If the chief of police station is a Muslim, then the police commander is a Serb. And was that done at all levels where officials are elected and appointed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the power sharing took place according to the following principle: All the different positions, offices, were listed, and then one side would choose a particular office, and then the other side had the right to choose another one. And it all went on that way until all of the offices were distributed, all the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct that all of this functioned properly, more or less, until the cessation of Slovenia and Croatia -- or, rather, until they held their referendums and when these tensions broke out in the western part of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be it roughly. The reason was that there were organised departures of Muslims from Bratunac. The SDA organised their trips to Croatia where they joined the ZNG and fought against the Serb people. Not a single case was recorded of a Muslim representative of the people going and fighting on the side of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or on the side of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or on the side of Yugoslavia. You can put it that way as well. That disrupted the relationship between the two coalition partners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness D387.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the chief of police in Bratunac was Senad Hodzic on behalf of the SDA? He was a Muslim who was there on behalf of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Senad Hodzic was chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to take a look at this document, and the second paragraph reads as follows: "In keeping with that, in a letter to the Bratunac Municipal Secretariat of National Defence, we requested a list of the free military conscripts according to local communes, respecting the ethnic structure." So in the first paragraph, a 100 per cent increase in the police force was ordered. Did you hear about that? And this caused some degree of suspicion among the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in the second paragraph it says that they asked the military department to say who was free out of the military conscripts, and then it says: "After we received the requested list and started making the necessary checks, we obtained information that the list included a certain number of Muslim military conscripts who have spent time in Croatia on a part of the training within the MUP of Croatia. We do not know on whose orders or recommendation, but it is believed that Serb citizens do not have enough trust in such future members of the reserve police force," and so on and so forth. Do you agree that this Muslim, the chief of the public security station, acted professionally, that he did not send these people because he knew and believed that that would have been detrimental for relations in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was still believed that co-existence could continue in Bratunac in harmony. I understand the chief of the public security station when he made this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in the town of Bratunac itself relations were is rather civilised and proper, whereas in villages extremism started to flourish and there was less of that in town?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a fact. And I think that I could safely say that that went both for the Serbs and the Muslims. In town that was certainly not the case, or, if so, to a very small degree. People who had radical views, groups that had radical views, ethnically speaking, all came from rural areas. There were even cases when they tried to impose these ideas within the town itself in a violent manner. One such situation was when a group of extremists, extreme nationalists from Voljavica, entered town chanting, This is Bosnia. They were firing their guns into the air intimidating both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Voljavica a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voljavica is a Muslim village exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that already at the end of August or September, the 1st of September, a crisis broke out when the JNA wanted to take its documentation from the military department in the municipality, and about 10.000 Muslims assembled there and made that impossible?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put it this way: That that was one of the key moments that disrupted the coalition government of the SDS and the SDA, and at the same time it disrupted relations between the two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By then, were tensions felt in Bratunac, tensions that stemmed from what was happening on the political scene, primarily the efforts made by the SDA and other Muslim parties to have Bosnia secede from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there were other options that were there, and it was believed that Bosnia would remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that throughout July and August there were debates in the public that were well known and that there was this agreement between the Muslims and Serbs that was reached? It was Adil Zulfikarpasic and Muhamed Filipovic that spoke on behalf of the Muslims, and this was an historic Serb-Muslim agreement. Is that what you meant, because that envisaged that Bosnia would remain within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I meant, because I know of this agreement and I believed it. I believed that we would remain in a single state after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that we relented and allowed for the possibility of Bosnia to secede on the condition that we are not out-voted, and that what was envisaged within that context was the establishment of two municipalities in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, too. I know that in the municipality of Bratunac, with the agreement of the SDA and the SDS, there was a commission that worked on the division of the territory of the municipality of Bratunac to see where the Muslim majority was and where the Serb majority was. In our area villages were either majority Muslim or majority Serb; whereas the town itself was split half and half, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that negotiations progressed very well and that in the Serb part of town, in the Serb villages, the Serbs would have their own authorities, and in the Muslim villages, in the Muslim part of town, the Muslims would have their own authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, that was the kind of division that exist nowadays. In some towns there are several different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So a large part of the town infrastructure would remain shared, and things would function like in a town with several municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1405. Could we have that, please, along with my apologies for the delay in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is already admitted as D297 with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you from the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have the Serbian version in Cyrillic. It's handwritten. Actually, could you please scroll up so that we see the bottom of the page, because there's a stamp there, the Serbian version. Do you agree that what it says here is the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serb municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that whenever a municipality had the prefix "Serb," it meant that in that town there was also a Muslim municipality and perhaps even a Croat municipality, too, that this does not mean that all of Bratunac is a Serb municipality; rather, it is only part of Bratunac that is the Serb municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question with any degree of certainty. This is the stamp of the Serb municipality of Bratunac from the time when it was expected that there would be a division of town in administrative terms into two municipality, because we had two ethnic groups, two peoples in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page to see what kind of conclusions were reached then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the last page. Let's see page 1. In B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here in paragraph 1 that representatives of both peoples accept as a reality that the division process is a reality and inevitable and agreed that it can be realised in a peaceful and democratic way?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, it says that the establishment of a Serb public security station in Bratunac and the division of the existing public security station is the first step in that direction. Is it correct that the Muslim police remained in the existing building, whereas the Serb police selected another building as their temporary base?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't need to read out all of this, but you please take a look. Everything should be done in a democratic way, schools should start working again and all inhabitants return. Does that mean that before the conflict broke out the population left, people belonging to both faiths?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone expel them or were they fearful of the way things were developing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were leaving town for security reasons, because the security situation had deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now in Serbian. I believe -- yes, yes. Paragraph 11. In English we should also look at the next page. Eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "Equal numbers of Serb and Muslim policemen should be engaged." Was that a measure to deal with the tension and suspicions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To establish parity, so that no one would feel threatened. Say if there were two times more policemen belonging to one ethnic group or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on it says in 13 that the plans and tasks should be co-ordinated by both chiefs and that joint on-site investigations should be conducted, and so on and so forth. And the last paragraph says that disputes and problems should be resolved in a peaceful and democratic way; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was the Serb side enthusiastic about the establishment of two municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb side was primarily interested in avoiding conflicts and in having problems resolved in a peaceful manner. One of the ways in which these problems could be resolved was what we saw, namely, the split into two administrative entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it envisaged, was there any idea and would it be possible to realise it that Muslims should be expelled from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That wouldn't work. That couldn't be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They would get the same things that the Serbs did. They would have their own policemen, their administration, and so on and so forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break for 50 minutes and resume at 1.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.42 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, I'll try to go through this as fast as possible, the things that happened in 1991 and the beginning of 1992. In paragraphs 11 -- or, rather, 13 through 16, you spoke about Crisis Staffs, even in 8 as well, the Crisis Staff of the party. Do you agree that there is a distinction between a Crisis Staff of the party that can only provide information and the Crisis Staff of the municipality that consists of people from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16, you say that you did not know what the criteria were, but it was formed as stated in the instructions: "Some people became members of the Crisis Staff based on the duties they already performed." That's paper A and B, those instructions, we'll get to that later? Let me ask you another thing: In our country, in our culture, if you will, that before and after situation like this, for example, the snow that fell now, when there's a crisis, the -- all the potentials of the state are mobilised and called a Crisis Staff, say when there's a flood or when there's a lack of electricity, any kind of crisis. Do the authorities focus then and start functioning as a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Whenever a state of emergency is imposed. And I came to testify now from that kind of a situation, when a state of emergency was imposed because of the snowfall. Crisis Staffs are established, and they operate for as long as the state of emergency is in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that for 20 years, until 2011, you were convinced that the meeting of the Municipal Board of the SDS on the 23rd of December, 1991, was convened because of something that was the result of some agreement with Izetbegovic or a result of the conference, and then someone offered you the possibility that this meeting had been convened because of paper A and B; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to this question would be I do not remember, because I got a document that was authentic from the session of the Municipal Board, that is. The document is actually the minutes of that meeting. It includes the agenda, and basically I confirmed the authenticity of that document which shows what it was that was discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a person who organised and technically prepared meetings, would you agree that usually the reason for convening a meeting is stated in the first item on the agenda and then the other items follow? So it would be compulsory to have this in item one, and the rest is optional; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And the last item is miscellaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us cast a glance at the agenda in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call it up? Can the Prosecution assist us with this? It's a document of theirs. It's been admitted as a P document, the meeting of the 23rd of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it P2598, appearing in para 15?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find it. Sorry about that. P2598. Yes, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have 15, para 15, in front of us, minutes of 23rd of December, P2598.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you say -- I'm going to read it out in English because they'll interpret it better that way: [In English] "I was shown minutes of 23rd of December, 1991, and asked what I remember about the meeting and the instructions presented to the board. These minutes are accurate, as far as I can recall. I was also shown a document entitled 'Instructions for the Organisation and Activity of Organs of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a State of Emergency,' dated 19th of December, 1991." [Interpretation] So a bit further down you say: [In English] [As read] "when I was first asked about these instructions at my interview in May 2011, I first thought they related to agreement between Karadzic and Izetbegovic. Having reviewed them and refreshed my memory, it is clear that the instructions were not based on any agreement with Izetbegovic. Rather, those were instructions from the SDS party leadership on what to do and how to react in 20 -- in a certain conditions and -- at that time." [Interpretation] Let us now take a look at D86, 00086, that is, and see -- actually, we can see it here as well. Item 1 on the agenda, yes. A decision was made to establish a Serbian B and H. Yes, that's it. So the first item says that a decision was made to establish a Serbian B and H; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this decision was not made at a party meeting held on the 19th of December but rather at the Assembly of the Serb people on the 21st of December?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the date, but the decision to establish a Serb BH was established -- was made at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at D00086. In Serbian, it's page 28. Maybe -- maybe 28. Actually, let's see. 152 are the last three digits of the ERN number. And in English it's 14. One page further up in Serbian, please. And in English it's page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, sorry, on the first page, it says: "The 4th session of the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 21st of December, 1991." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in Serbian and in English page 14. Yes. Please. Take a look at the bottom of the page. Could we see the bottom of the English version and this one. It says here: "Proceeding from the constitutional right of peoples to self-determination, the Serb -- the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the session held on the 21st of December, 1991, is adopting a decision to establish a Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And we see that in English as well. Is it clearer to you now that this meeting on the 23rd was convened in relation to this, not in relation to what had happened on the 19th? Does it look more logical to you now that this was the reason, not what happened on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not remember, but it's possible that this was it, bearing in mind the item on the agenda and this event that had to do with the establishment of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it likely that during that meeting Variants A or B were discussed? Did you see a registration number, a signature, or a stamp on Variant A or B?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that. I remember the instructions, and I remember -- I remember that there were variants where the Serb people were a minority, and then there were others where the Serb people were a majority. We were in a situation that meant that we were in a minority, because the Serb population in the territory of the municipality of Bratunac was a minority then. That is to say that the second variant applied in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Crisis Staff and the party was formed a bit earlier in 1992 and in the municipality perhaps only on the 2nd or the 3rd of April when it was obvious that there would be a war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bratunac was established after the Crisis Staff of the party was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're dealing with these paragraphs, paragraph 18 refers to a meeting held in the party on the 24th of February, 1992, and I'm going to read it out in English so that it's interpreted better: [In English] [As read] "At first I could not recall this meeting [indiscernible], but now that I read the document, those events from that time have started to come back to me. The outcome of this meeting and the measures discussed at that meeting, that is the implementation of the measures of the second level of the instructions were not something that was typical just for Bratunac, rather, this meeting and the outcome something that was -- was essentially the result of the overall situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina just transposed to Bratunac." [Interpretation] Now, that's the document that they showed you, but do you remember somehow things developed, and do you remember that the SDA was negotiating but also preparing for war and that this solution was indispensable as a measure aimed at protection against a Muslim attack?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the first measure that we introduced was duty service and providing information to local boards about the situation in general and the security situation in the municipality. When the situation worsened, then President Deronjic scheduled this meeting, and then another measure was introduced that had to do with the security situation at the time, the situation that had deteriorated. In order to overcome that, guards -- or guard duty was introduced, and the suggestion made was for the population to obtain food supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that Serbs and Muslims guarded their apartment buildings together, whereas in villages they all had their own guards?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's how it was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this phase two was introduced into various municipalities at different times based on their own local assessments? Do you recall that there was any instruction to the effect, Now you are to implement this and now you should implement that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My apologies. We didn't have the interpretation. Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic -- or we didn't hear the interpretation of the previous answer from Mr. Katanic. Could you repeat your answer kindly, Mr. Katanic, to the question: "Do you recall that there was any instruction to the effect, Now you are to implement this and now you should implement that?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was just that one instruction that we implemented. As for any subsequent instructions or monitoring of how those instructions were being implemented, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as I'm moving through these paragraphs, would you please look at paragraph 19. You were shown minutes from a meeting of February 1st, 1993 - that's 65 ter 00593 - and then it goes on to say what was said at that meeting. Is it correct that because of the police failure to maintain law and order and fight looting, a request came from me -- or, rather, from us to actually vote on confidence in the authorities? So to take a vote of confidence in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that there was any request for a vote of confidence on the then-government, but I do remember the meeting. I organised it, and we also had guests who were invited to attend that meeting or the Assembly session. And the reason was that one of the items on the agenda was this vote of confidence, a vote of confidence in the Municipal Board and the authorities in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the party was trying to check whether those people who were in authority, whether they were doing their job properly and whether they still enjoyed trust?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, at this meeting, which could be interpreted to be in the function of the pre-election period, was that used in order to actually bring into question those people who were in -- in power at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The introductory remarks by Mr. Deronjic could be interpreted as bragging, which was not unusual -- which was not unusual in situations of a vote of confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when this vote of confidence was taken, did some people actually gain -- retain their positions and some people had to resign?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody was voted in except for the chief of police, Mr. Luka, who was voted out because in the preceding period, it was found that there had been a lot of crime and that they -- the crimes could have been prevented had more effort been put into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then subsequent to this, he resigned; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was replaced by Ljubisa Borovcanin. And as for him, I don't know if he resigned or whether he was just fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that you had occasion to experience the situation where the Muslim formations, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, created an atmosphere of insecurity, because there were a lot of incidents on the eve of the war which contributed to the exacerbation of the crisis. There were several incidents, some people were killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned the case where a group of Muslims from Voljavica came into town and intimidated the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember as of 21st of March that there were several attacks, and all this is from the Muslim sources on the 24th March in Buljim; 25th of March, Orahovac and Bukova Glava; and 25th of March in Zeleni Jadar where allegedly ten Chetniks were killed. Do you remember that in Zeleni Jadar, before the month of April, some workers, some forestry workers were killed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that until April 15th -- or before April 15th there was an offensive on Konjevic Polje? Do you remember that on the 3rd of April a JNA depot was blown up, a JNA depot in Nova Kasaba? Was this a crisis situation, and before the 17th of April, did they have an initiative?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but there are, I think, four or five questions in that. I don't know how the witness can keep up. I certainly cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't need an answer to these individual incidents. Now, do you agree with me that at that time the Party of Democratic Action was the one who actually created this crisis, critical situation with all these incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do recall some situations where some radical Muslim elements intimidated the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 17th of April, is it correct that some saviours all of a sudden appeared, some members of paramilitary groups, that they took control of Bratunac, they suspended the Assembly and took over?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they appear -- did they make the first appearance as volunteers and then they became renegades from the JNA, and they were in villages and towns, but they were not anywhere in the woods?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they first came to town, they presented themselves as volunteers of the Serbian people, and they came to help. They came armed, and any group that had arms was an armed force and wanted to take power, which created major difficulties for the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed, and you mentioned this in your statement, but also in the interview you confirmed that the authorities immediately tried to get rid of these volunteers and that people became anxious and upset, especially the women, who -- because the men had already joined the army, because they felt that they would be threatened because of these volunteers, by Muslim extremists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They even organised a protest rally in front of the municipal building, these women, and they physically attacked the president of the Executive Committee, Radoljub Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the SDS, and he was opposed to these paramilitary groups; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The decision was taken at the Crisis Staff meeting, a decision that these volunteers were no longer welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your interview, you said that the authorities would have gotten rid of them and opposed them had they had the strength and the power, and that in Bratunac five to ten armed men already represented an armed force for the authorities the way they were.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters cannot hear the speaker clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read this out in English, because we're not happy with the interpretation of what the witness said: [In English] "Yes, the decision was taken at the Crisis Staff meeting, a decision that these volunteers were no longer welcome." [Interpretation] Were they ever welcome?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, they were welcomed, because the Serb people had already been scared because of the Muslim extremists who made their appearance from time to time from the rural areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that they were welcome when they said that they were JNA volunteers but that the welcome was withdrawn when they stopped being JNA volunteers, when they reneged and become an independent armed force?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We considered every volunteer to be welcome if they were at the disposal of the JNA at the time when it was in Bratunac or if they joined the Bratunac Brigade, which was later established. All those who came on their own and acted in their own interest, they were not welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 24, there's talk about disarming, and it is described that this was done by the Yugoslav People's Army. Can we agree that the Yugoslav People's Army was a legitimate force all the way until the 19th of May, 1992, whereas in this paragraph the date mentioned is the 19th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall by what time the Yugoslav People's Army was considered a legitimate force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it's documented, and, as such, it is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this paragraph you talk about parts of the Novi Sad Corps that were stationed there on their way -- on their way back from Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the commander was Captain Reljic, and that this unit collected weapons that were held by civilians. Now, do we agree that in our system, according to the Tito doctrine, an armed populous, the doctrine -- the doctrine of an armed populous meant that any worker, any factory, had arms and could be armed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The doctrine was that the entire population was the army. That was the doctrine from the previous Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this paragraph you say that the weapons were collected in local communities, and then in the last sentence it says: [In English] "In practice, only the Muslims were being disarmed." [Interpretation] Now, I would like to ask you this, and I would like you to tell us what your position is: Was the crucial question here their -- or was the determining factor their faith or the fact that they refused to respond to the mobilisation call-up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Religious affiliation had nothing to do with it. In 1991, the SDA organised an attempt to prevent the JNA to collect the military booklets of all conscripts in the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was a sign to the JNA that the people in Bratunac did not gather spontaneously but that they were organised.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. They were organised. The SDA invited the Muslim people not to respond to JNA call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the Crisis Staff in Bratunac also had a negative position on the formation and arming of paramilitary formations irrespective of religious affiliation or ethnicity. To that end, I would like to call up 1D4094, a document of the Crisis Staff. So no distinction was made in terms of ethnicity or religion. Whoever was part of a TO, JNA unit, was part of the legitimate armed force, whereas the rest were not. 1D4094, 1D4094. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the cover page. It reads: "Order forbidding all paramilitary formations to be active in the territory of Bratunac municipality." I think the second page is empty. Perhaps we can move to the third page immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom it in, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that as early as the 1st of May, the Crisis Staff used a Cyrillic typewriter? That is to say, the Serb municipality forbade the existence and activity of all paramilitary formations in the municipality of Bratunac. Is that the gist of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And not only paramilitary formations but individuals as well; that is to say people who possessed weapons illegally and were -- and were active on their own.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2060, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 2060. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 3rd or 4th of May in Hranca a JNA convoy was stopped withdrawing towards Yugoslavia? It was attacked and several young soldiers were killed? Is Hranca in the outskirts of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hranca is 2 kilometres away from Bratunac. There was an incident at that time, but I no longer remember details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Judge Zekic was killed on the 8th of May? And as you have described him, he had been a prominent person. As you say in paragraph 27, he was a judge and an Assembly deputy. He was killed on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Goran Zekic enjoyed the trust of the Serb people not only in Srebrenica, because he hailed from Srebrenica, but he enjoyed the trust of the people of the whole region. As you probably know, he was a people's deputy in the B and H Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You had -- you informed us that you had an objection to paragraph 26 and the way operation Glogova was described, where it was called an attack. You said you believed it to be -- to have been directed at disarming the people who caused a number of incidents we referred to previously.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to expand on this so as not to say yes or no only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Feel free.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in that operation as a TO member. Mr. Miroslav Deronjic was with me in the same capacity, in civilian clothes. We were told that it was our task to guard a perimeter towards Glogova on the Srebrenica side in case someone tried to flee with weapons to Srebrenica. It was the last thing on my mind that it was supposed to be an attack on Glogova, because any attack would have to commence with artillery fire followed by the infantry. We were not ready or trained for that. Simply, our task was to guard the line so that no one could flee with weapons. The JNA, which was trusted by the Serb people, entered Glogova on a -- on a paved road. They arrived in the centre of Glogova with the aim of disarming the people who had not handed in their weapons. It was assessed that there were a lot of weapons in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You didn't know then that there were going to be some killings, and even after the fact you were still unaware of it for a while?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I can say to that is it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You discussed that in paragraphs 37 and 38, as well as 39. In paragraph 38 you say: [In English] "I have been told that what Deronjic stated and pled guilty to is that the purpose of the Glogova operation was to remove the Muslim population of Glogova from Bratunac municipality. That is the conclusion I, myself, made after the operation, but that is not something I knew during the operation." [Interpretation] Paragraph 37, the last sentence is: "[In English] My assumption at the time was that the purpose of the operation was to gather people and not to expel them." [Interpretation] In your opinion, what Mr. Deronjic pleaded guilty to, does it stray from everything you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that the aim was to expel the Muslim population from Glogova, which is something Mr. Deronjic pleaded guilty to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he confess that to you before he did to the Court or did you only learn of the fact of his plea following the fact here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only learned of it once he pleaded guilty to it before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on there was another group -- well, Makedonac was part of the first group at the beginning of the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they beat up people, slapped people around, tied up prominent citizens and paraded them through town; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't Makedonac's group that did that. It was done by the group where Mijovic was later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, so it's the second group. They also terrorised; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you escorted Mr. Deronjic at a meeting where he sought my support and the support of others to have the group driven out of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That was after they began detaining people in their premises. And the people they detained were not only ordinary citizens but also members of the both civilian and military authorities. They detained them and physically mistreated them. Even Mr. Deronjic was detained, and physically mistreated, as well as I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 53, you say that they even put a gun to your head and that they mistreated you and that your life was in danger; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not pertain to the group commanded by Mijovic. He threatened to kill Mr. Deronjic, even took him to the Drina River to kill him there, but it turned out to be intimidation only, to put pressure on him. I was threatened with a gun by the group where Makedonac was when I tried to have several Muslim families evacuated from Bratunac. One of the Muslims involved was my best man, Edhem Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Serbs at the time, the Serbs from Bratunac, were trying to protect the Bratunac Muslims from these people and that it was very dangerous to attempt that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that it was dangerous. Despite that, many Serbs decided to help their co-citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you managed, or, one of your relatives managed to save several people; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be quite a list of such examples. I'll only mention one. The Defence commander in Kravica smuggled out a person by the name of Ahmic in the trunk of his car. His nickname was Siledzija. He took him to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the next day, he safely escorted him to the territory controlled by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 41, you say that you were asked whether Muslims were forced to leave Bratunac municipality, and you said that they had no choice, because if they had stayed, they probably would have been mistreated and even killed. Can we agree that they were driven away by fear and the events themselves, or were they driven out by the authorities who knocked on their doors and said, Pack up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the best answer to that question would be if I said that if I were Muslim, I, too, would have left Bratunac most likely, as it was unsafe to be Muslim in the town, and the authorities had no means to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said something similar about Srebrenica 1995, and I will find where exactly, where you say that no one told them that they should leave, that they had the option to remain. So were they told that they could not be protected or did they reach that conclusion themselves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the decision taken by representatives of the Muslim people. They probably consulted with their own people and decided to leave Srebrenica, although they also had the option to remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a look at 1D4104. This is a review of the various important decisions and orders issued by the War Presidency and the Crisis Staff of Bratunac municipality. It was published -- 4104. 1D4104. This is not the document. Can we now see the next page, and I'd like to see whether you remember that these were the decisions by the municipal authorities and that this was their position. The English is okay. No, we need the B/C/S, the Serbian page. For instance, the third from the top: "Decision to disarm civilians who possess weapons in Bratunac municipality," and this really applied to Serbs more than to Muslims in September 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now see the next page, please. Here it says: "Decision for all paramilitary formations to leave Bratunac municipality," and this was on the 6th of May, two days before the killing of Goran Zekic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then let's skip the next one, and then we see the one after that is a decision to accommodate refugees from Srebrenica and other municipalities, and here already we see that we're on the 8th of May. Could you tell us what the flow of refugees looked like in Bratunac, and how did that affect the safety and security of both Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the refugees began arriving, there were -- or, actually, the influx of refugees came in waves. They did not all arrive at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that it says here that they will be accommodated in abandoned houses temporarily while they're engaged by Bratunac TO. They must maintain and secure the houses where they're accommodated with all the property found there. In other words, they were not given that property. They were just allowed to use it temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The abandoned houses had been registered by the municipal authorities and sealed off. Later on, they were used to accommodate refugees pursuant to this decision on the proviso that they should maintain and secure all the -- the house and the property there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next page, please. Here toward the bottom in Serbian we see there's an order to prohibit the operation of all paramilitary units in the municipality. That is a decision of May 1st, 1992, that we've already seen. Can we see the next page, please. During this period, is it correct that it was impossible to get from Bratunac to Pale? The only way out, the only open route, was to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was possible to get to Pale, but it was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's take a look at this, an order prohibiting the serving and use of alcohol in Bratunac municipality; order prohibiting looting, smuggling and corruption; order on temporarily accommodating refugees and uncared-for individuals in abandoned houses and buildings; and then at the bottom, order prohibiting bringing alcohol to the territory. So were all these measures and decisions taken in order to improve the security and safety of citizens?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As I've already said, I was a member -- I was the owner of the Caesar cafe, and at the time, it was prohibited to serve hard liquor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would I like to tend this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it as Exhibit D2061. In the meantime, Mr. Karadzic, for the planning purpose, can I ask how much longer you need.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that I can complete by ten minutes past 3.00, but perhaps I'll be able to do it even sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have re-examination, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I have up to ten minutes and it might be shortened as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, sorry, I just need literally one minute at the end of the session to address a matter in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could the Registrar approach the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll sort out a way to deal with it, but in the meantime please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 77, you talk about -- and I will read it out for better interpretation, the third line: [In English] "I am convinced that there would have been a will by the police bodies to protect the Muslim population who would have stayed in Srebrenica, but despite this will, I do not believe that police would have been in a position to offer a guarantee that the Muslim population would have been safe and secure." [Interpretation] But they weren't told, Stay, but we can't guarantee your safety. Rather, your conclusion was that the police was not very strong; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The police was strong and powerful, but the situation was such that I don't believe that they would have been able to prevent possible acts of vengeance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You speak about possible acts of vengeance because of what had been happening the previous three years; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were the Muslims themselves afraid that this might happen even to those people who had not committed any crimes or atrocities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that -- I believe that that was one of the main reasons when people assessed this decision and when they made this decision to leave Srebrenica. I believe that was the strongest reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll continue until 3.00, and if necessary, we'll have another 15 minutes after having a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so. I will do my best to complete by 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about an incident of 1995, or, rather, the events in the school. It was shown here, and I want to check whether you knew anything about it, it was said here that on the 14th, after the prisoners were evacuated from the school, bodies were found in every of the -- every one of the 16 classrooms. There would be one or two or up to three bodies, which would mean that there would be up to 60 people -- 60 dead bodies there. Do you know whether they had been killed after the evacuation of most of the prisoners or were they killed during the incarceration and detention?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard of the events in the school. I heard about that later on from my family or relatives, because we live in the vicinity of that building, very close to it. I did not know the scale of the incident and the crime there that occurred at the school, but I asked around. I asked the people who knew about it, and I learnt that there were about 30 dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of any information whether they were killed while they were detained, or were they brought in the course of the night and then killed one, two, or three per classroom, because I'm a bit confused. If they were killed, why would that be done in multiple classrooms if they were brought to one place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. All I heard was that there had been an incident, that a group had tried to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that they were killed in their attempt to escape and then their bodies brought -- taken back to the classrooms?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 56, you recall that I visited Srebrenica on the 4th of August, 1995. Do you remember whether this was a religious event and that I did not come to the municipal building, nor did I go anyplace else?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that event. Mr. Deronjic asked me to clear up an office at the cultural centre where we could receive you, where you could visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that we walked to the church together. Now, what was the -- what was the condition, the state of this church in Srebrenica when we got there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not accompany you to the church, and I don't know what kind of condition it was in. I know that it had been devastated, but I don't know to what extent. I remained -- I returned to Bratunac while you attended -- there was some kind of ritual, I don't know what to call it, because there was a very religious woman there who had a vision of some sort, and she said that there should be a cross put up in the Old Town, and the cross should face some other town, I don't know exactly which one, which would then protect this area and the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So was this the lifting of the cross a tradition that dates all the way back to Emperor Constantine and his mother, the Empress Helena?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, but I do know that this happened as I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 98, you talk about reburials, and you say that you were asked in October -- in September and October 1995 -- or, rather, whether in September or October 1995 you issued some quantities of fuels meant for some reburials. I will read it out in English: [In English] "I did not, but as a citizen and as many other citizens, I could notice that these bodies were relocated from Glogova." [Interpretation] So am I correct if I say that somewhere in Glogova, and you don't know the exact location, people who had been killed in Glogova were buried in May 1992, and that in July 1995, at least everyone who died then, who was killed then, was buried in Glogova as well as the victims from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be assumed that there were victims in Glogova from both 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the civilian protection had the duty to sanitise the terrain throughout the war and that after every battle the civilian protection would have to bury both our and enemy soldiers? Well, not in the woods but in towns.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that the perpetrators of these crimes openly bragged about these things, or was it your impression that they were trying to conceal this from the authorities, that they made an effort to conceal it from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident discussed there, the relocation of the bodies, that is something that I did not see. I did not see the bodies on the trucks, but I did see the trucks, and I heard comments of my fellow citizens that bodies were being relocated from Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I meant in general terms, any crimes. Did the perpetrators move around freely and bragged about them, or did they try to conceal it from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one would want to brag about crimes they committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the authorities, the police, and the military command, they were unaware because this was concealed from them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one committed a crime, I know that they could not publicly brag about having committed that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katanic. I'm trying my best to return before your daughter's birthday. I'd like to thank you for your testimony, and give my regards to Bratunac town.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you were just asked about this visit of Mr. Karadzic's to Srebrenica on August 4th. You remember that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was General Krstic in Srebrenica on that visit as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. The other issue that I wanted to address, Mr. President, is -- regards the transcript today, at page 39 and 40, when we were discussing the witness's paragraphs 92 and 93, and there was a discussion as to whether it was a leading question from the interview or not. You were part of that discussion. I have those two pages from the transcript, from those two pages in order to admit them, which is what I would like to do. I will have to play the audio which is about seven minutes. If the Defence does not object to the admission of those two pages then I don't have to play the audio and I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, actually, we don't object. We think it would be useful for the Chamber to have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is 65 ter 23612, and it's page -- it's just two pages. Yeah. So it's two pages. Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, you talked about the brick factory. Mr. Beara and Mr. Deronjic went together to the place and there was debate whether prisoners could be imprisoned there or not. Have you been to the place ever?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain to us -- to us how it looks like, what -- how big it is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of an area, it is quite large. As for the buildings themselves, it doesn't have any specific structures that would have a roof. There's only the administrative building and the workshop itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us how big is the administrative building and workshop. How many employees are working there, or how many rooms or offices does it have?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You said that's the only building that has a roof.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a small building. In terms of size, I believe it can accommodate up to ten office workers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever been to Sase mine?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, but I wasn't at the brickworks during the war or in the Sase mine during the war. I only visited the locations before and after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to me as well about the Sase mine in terms of building or size.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sase mine had buildings that were much larger than the ones at the brickworks in Bratunac, although I can't tell you with any certainty what the size was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You told me just now that you believed that the building at brick factory could accommodate up to ten office workers. How about the office building in Sase mine?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KATANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's much bigger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? The witness meant to say ten offices rather than ten workers per se, because ten workers can be placed in a single office if needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. I put it well. The administrative building in the brick factory is small, and in normal conditions it cannot accommodate more than ten office employees. It has only three or four rooms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. Unless my colleagues have questions for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Katanic. On behalf of this Trial Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, we will rise all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. If you could excuse yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Should we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is now adjourned. We will resume on Monday at 9.00.
